Title: [Excerpt from] “Snow Machines: Venture Farther and Faster into the Wild on a Snowmobile”
Author: by Aaron Derr
Content: Just as there are different kinds of hiking, there are different kinds of snowmobiling.

Some sledheads are in it for the steep climbs. Others have the need for speed. And still others just like to use their snowmobiles to get away from it all, exploring areas that would be too difficult to access any other way.
That's Venturing Crew `115`. In the warm-weather `text(months)`, they travel from their homes near Snoqualmie, Washington, to paddle down their region's rivers and lakes in kayaks...
:box:Venturing Crew `115` = a group of teens connected to the Boy Scouts of America that participates in outdoor activities

Each winter, they return to the same spot — near snow-covered Swan Lake Campground— for an event they call Snowcamp. With its thick, high brush, that spot would be terrible for camping during the summer.
During winter, with around `text(12 feet)` of snow, it's practically paradise.
Fall Preparation
Snowcamp is in the middle of `text(February)`. But prep work starts `text(months)` earlier.
In `text(November)` and `text(December)`, the crew hosts its most effective fundraiser: Christmas-tree sales. Proceeds help pay for the maintenance of their fleet of `24` snowmobiles.

After the holidays, the Venturers get to work on their sleds. Those snowmobiles aren't going to take care of themselves, after all. They call them work parties, and they have them `text(three)` times a `text(week)`.

By `text(late January)` or `text(early February)`, the snowmobiles and crew are ready to go. The crew conducts training exercises on a snow-covered airfield. It's nice and flat and wide open-perfect for beginners and those who need to brush up on their skills....
Winter Camping
Once the Venturers are comfortable on the equipment, they're ready for Snowcamp. They start by hauling the snowmobiles and camping gear as far as they can into the wilderness until the road ends.

From there, they board their machines with tow-behind equipment sleds and drive several `text(miles)` farther. During their trek, they keep in touch with each other using `text(two-way)` radios built into their helmets. When they get to their spot — about `text(5,000 feet)` above sea level — they begin setting up camp.

`text(First)`, they mark the spot where they will have their fire. Then they mark a `text(40-foot)` diameter around that spot. Then they lay down a firewood platform and set firewood on top of that. As the fire burns, the platform drops deeper and deeper into the snow, at the rate of about `text(1 foot per hour)`.

In the meantime, the Scouts build a wall of ice blocks around the circle. (Imagine a `text(40-foot-wide)` igloo without a roof.) As the fire drops, the Venturers carve rows of stairs and benches into the snow.

After `12` or so `text(hours)`, the fire has sunk down — surrounded by walls that are now more than `text(8 feet)` high and an icy bowl `text(12 feet)` deep. It's like a miniature coliseum, and it's the perfect winter shelter — protected from the wind and warmed by the fire...
:box:coliseum = large outdoor theater

After spending the night in `text(four-season)` tents and igloos, the Venturers spend the `text(next day)` exploring the area on their snowmobiles. They often snowmobile up to a radio tower that offers sparkling views of the surrounding countryside...

To stay warm, they dress in layers and wear noncotton clothing. If you don't like to wear wool, you don't get to go snowmobiling. The crew spends several `text(weeks)` taking classes on proper winter clothing and how to stay warm in the cold environment...

After `text(three)` nights in the woods, the crew returns home. They are usually able to get back to the same spot the very next weekend for another `text(three)` nights. If weather permits, they might have `text(one)` more snowmobile trip in the spring.
Then they store the snowmobiles for the summer and look forward to the `text(next year's)` Snowcamp.
